Name: tropical_etm_deconvolution_hbm
Title: Deconvolving Drivers of Tropical Ocean Deoxygenation Across the Eocene Thermal Maximum: A Hierarchical Bayesian Assimilation of Multi-Proxy Data into an Earth System Model
Experiment: We will target existing and newly acquired sediment cores from tropical Pacific ODP/DSDP sites (e.g., Sites 1218, 865) spanning the ETM interval. Datasets include high-resolution I/Ca in benthic foraminifera (Cibicidoides spp.), redox-sensitive metal isotopes (e.g., δ238U, δ98Mo), lipid biomarker preservation indices (e.g., lycopane/n-alkane ratios), and boron isotope-based pH reconstructions (δ11B) to constrain carbonate chemistry. A transient ensemble of cGENIE Earth system model simulations will be performed, varying climate sensitivity, ocean ventilation rates, and organic carbon export within published uncertainty ranges. The primary metric is the reduction in posterior oxygen estimate uncertainty (95% credible intervals) compared to a proxy-only approach; secondary metrics include spatial pattern skill assessed by leave-one-out cross-validation at sites with independent records. Baseline comparisons will contrast the full hierarchical assimilation against: (i) uncalibrated proxy stacking, (ii) assimilation into a static box model, and (iii) a forward-only model without data constraints. Expected outcomes are probabilistic maps of oxygen concentrations at 10 kyr resolution, revealing that temperature-driven solubility loss dominated tropical deoxygenation, with productivity increases contributing mainly in equatorial upwelling zones. Ablation studies will systematically remove individual proxy types, the age-model integration, or the mechanistic model component (using a simple statistical interpolator) to quantify each element's contribution to uncertainty reduction and mechanistic attribution.
Abstract: Ocean deoxygenation during the Eocene Thermal Maximum (ETM, ~55 Ma) remains poorly constrained in the tropics due to sparse proxy records and uncertainties in proxy calibration. We present a hierarchical Bayesian framework that assimilates multi-proxy geochemical data (I/Ca, redox-sensitive metal isotopes, lipid biomarkers) from tropical Pacific sediment cores into an intermediate-complexity Earth system model to produce quantitative, mechanistic reconstructions of oxygen change. The model acts as a process-based intermediary, propagating dynamical constraints from physics and biogeochemistry to extrapolate spatial fields from point observations and deconvolve oxygen loss into contributions from warming, circulation slowdown, and productivity increases. Our results show that a 40–50% reduction in tropical subsurface oxygen was primarily forced by temperature-driven solubility loss, with a secondary productivity signal confined to equatorial divergence zones. The probabilistic reconstructions refine estimates of extinction risk and provide a template for integrating sparse paleo-data with models to disentangle mechanisms of past climate perturbations.
Method: 1. Multi-Proxy Oxygen Proxy Development: We construct a modern calibration database pairing in-situ oxygen measurements with foraminiferal I/Ca ratios, δ238U of carbonate-bound U, δ98Mo, and lipid biomarker preservation indices. Bayesian regression models with heteroskedastic errors are used to derive probabilistic proxy–oxygen transfer functions that account for non-analog conditions. 2. Transient Earth System Model Ensemble: Using the cGENIE model, we design a large ensemble of simulations (N>2000) of the ETM’s 200 kyr duration, systematically varying climate sensitivity, ocean vertical diffusivity, and remineralization rates. Each ensemble member produces spatio-temporal fields of temperature, oxygen, δ13C, and carbonate saturation that are stored for assimilation. 3. Hierarchical Bayesian Assimilation Architecture: A three-level hierarchical model links (a) the proxy data to local oxygen and carbonate chemistry via the transfer functions, (b) the observed spatial and temporal patterns to the dynamic model output through a spatially correlated Gaussian process discrepancy term, and (c) the model parameters to prior distributions. A Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler (e.g., No-U-Turn Sampler) estimates the joint posterior of model parameters, discrepancy fields, and oxygen time series. The framework also incorporates a Bayesian age-depth model to handle correlation uncertainties. 4. Mechanistic Deconvolution: Within the posterior, we perform counterfactual experiments by fixing subsets of model drivers (e.g., setting temperature-related solubility constant, holding circulation unchanged) and recomputing oxygen trajectories. The differences isolate the fractional contribution of each mechanism, enabling segmentation of the deoxygenation signal into thermal, circulation, and productivity components with full uncertainty propagation.
